A systematic review21 conclud- ed that prostaglandin E1 and its analogues, given intrave- nously or intra-arterially, were beneficial, but their use may not be practical in most patients.7 Oral prostaglandins such as beraprost have also been tried but do not appear to be effective and are not recommended.7,9,19 Topical dino- prostone has also been used. Other drugs that have shown positive results in small stud- ies include arginine,16 ginkgo biloba,15 glutathione,16 levo- carnitine,15,22 policosanol,16 and sulodexide.23 Growth factors24 (given locally) and gene therapy25 have also been tried. If intermittent claudication is severe, and does not respond to medical treatment, non-pharmacological techniques such as bypass surgery, endarterectomy, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, or intravascular stenting should be considered.7,9 After these procedures, treatment to pre- vent postoperative thrombosis and restenosis may be nec- essary (see Reperfusion and Revascularisation Proce- dures, p.1181). Sudden or acute arterial occlusion due to emboli or to thrombosis may occur in 10% of patients with atheroscle- rotic disease, but is rare in thromboangiitis obliterans.
